name: Kira Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we do not sell anything or campaign. What you say is confidential. Could you tell me about a normal workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am Kira Garcia, 58, and I do junior carpentry and general work on building sites. My partner and I have grown-up children, and I keep a small cloth around my folding rule so the markings stay clear in the dust.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you do most often on site?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I carry boards, hold frames and mark cuts while a carpenter checks my work. I like when a room is finished square, but it takes me longer to learn a new method if nobody shows me in person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a better order list is useful if it gets the right boards to the right room. I would still have the carpenter check the length before I cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of my hours are carrying, holding and marking pieces, so a small office change does not replace the work I do. The worry I already have is the mortgage, because we have less than a month put aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking the site days offered and ask the foreman about next week before leaving. If a week were short, I would mend my work trousers again instead of buying a new pair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not feel threatened by a little faster paperwork. I do feel the old money worry when a site day disappears from the schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check before cutting a board for a frame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the mark against the opening and ask the carpenter if the measurement seems off. A wrong cut wastes a board we may not have time to replace that day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your household do when one of those days is cancelled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I look at which bill is due first and delay something we can manage without. Our grown-up children have their own homes, so I do not count on their money.

say: I would say **a better order list** helps if it sends the right boards.
I would still ask the carpenter to **check the length** before I cut.
think: Most of my hours are **physical work**, so a small office change does not replace my tasks.
I have **thin savings**, and the mortgage already worries me.
do: Keep taking **offered site days** and ask about next week before leaving.
Mend my **work trousers** again instead of replacing them after a short week.
feel: I do not feel threatened by paperwork, but a **missing site day** brings back my money worry.
S0.quote: A wrong cut wastes a board we may not have time to replace that day.
fieldNote: She separates small **paperwork changes** from her physical site tasks.
**Thin savings** make cancelled shifts a present concern despite modest AI exposure.
She checks **boards against the opening** before cutting to avoid waste.

steps.text: Keep taking offered site days and ask about next week before leaving
Mend work trousers again rather than replace them after a short-pay week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say use a new list if it makes the order clearer, but someone should still check what arrives. I would not ask a junior worker to trust a screen more than the carpenter who sees the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not use AI now, and I would be slow with a new screen at first. If the office changes the written notes I sometimes help with, I might lose a small task, but that does not tell me whether there will be fewer whole site projects.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the new plan on paper while the supervisor shows me how it matches the room. I would keep doing the jobs I know until I had seen the screen work on a real delivery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel cautious because I do not learn a new screen quickly by myself. I would try it after a demonstration, but I cannot spare unpaid hours to practise at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to compare during the demonstration?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the written plan, the screen and the opening we measured. I do not want to learn a new screen by making a mistake with a delivery order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help you learn if the screen becomes part of the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need a supervisor to stand with me for the first few orders and let me ask questions. After that I could decide whether I can do it without help.

say: I would use **a clearer list** if someone checks what arrives.
I would not ask a junior worker to trust **the screen** more than the carpenter who sees the room.
think: I do not use AI, and I would be **slow with screens** at first.
I could lose **written-note tasks**, but I do not know whether whole site projects will fall.
do: Ask for the **paper plan** while the supervisor shows how the screen matches the room.
Keep doing **familiar site tasks** until I have seen the screen work on a delivery.
feel: I feel **cautious with new screens**, and cannot spare unpaid hours to practise at home.
S1.quote: I do not want to learn a new screen by making a mistake with a delivery order.
fieldNote: She resists learning alone but may try after a **hands-on demonstration**.
She does not infer fewer **whole site projects** from changed office notes.
**Few local alternatives** make a change of employer difficult for her.

steps.text: Keep doing current site work while the supervisor demonstrates the screen
Wait to use the screen alone until a real order is checked

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the computer work changes first and robots come later. I would not tell the crew that working with their hands protects them until 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI could do the measurements and planning notes I sometimes help with by 2028. I would be around 60 then, and I do not know whether my practical work will be enough to keep steady income until robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028, I would ask the carpenter to teach me one practical task I have not done before, like fitting an interior door. In 2029, I would ask about paid shifts and keep my mortgage payment ahead of any new tool purchase.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is a short time to get more confident at work. I can ask to learn, but I cannot count on finding enough paid days to replace a missing task.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grown-up children if your shifts fell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell them our household needs a little time to see what work is available. They have their own homes, so I would not ask them to take responsibility for my bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes because robots arrive three years after thinking AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A later robot date gives me time, but it does not buy me a job until then. I would use the years to learn practical tasks while checking whether local builders still offer shifts.

say: I would say **computer work changes first**, with robots coming later.
I would not call **hands-on work protection** until 2031.
think: I think AI could do **measurement and planning notes** by 2028.
I will be **around 60 in 2028**, and do not know if practical work will keep my income steady.
do: Ask the carpenter to teach me **interior door fitting** before 2028.
Ask about paid shifts in 2029 and keep **mortgage money** ahead of tool purchases.
feel: **Two years is short** to become more confident at work.
I cannot count on enough **paid days** to replace a missing task.
S2.quote: A later robot date gives me time, but it does not buy me a job until then.
fieldNote: She distinguishes the **2028 thinking change** from later physical robots.
At **61**, she still expects work and income to matter before retirement.
**Around 61 in 2029**, she cannot assume retirement income will cover the household.

steps.text: Learn interior door fitting from the carpenter before 2028
Ask about paid site shifts in 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years gives me more time to practise before AI takes the planning tasks. I would not say it makes the trade secure, because robots could still change the physical work in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be around 63 when the thinking change arrives, but age alone will not tell me when I can stop working. I would still need to know whether sites have paid tasks for me after planning moves to AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for supervised practice on door fitting or trim while the foreman can show me the steps. In 2032, I would ask builders what jobs they still hire for before paying for a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me prepare without rushing into a course I cannot afford. I still feel unsure because the robot date comes before I know what my retirement income would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask a carpenter to check while you practise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask them to check whether my frame is square before I fix it permanently. I have been slow with that measurement, and I would rather catch it before the wall is closed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a course worth paying for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need to hear that local builders actually use the skill and are hiring people to do it. If the answer is only that it might be useful, I would wait and keep asking for paid practice.

say: I would say **five years** gives me time to practise before AI takes planning tasks.
I would not call the trade **secure after 2034**.
think: I will be **around 63 in 2031**, but age alone will not tell me when I can stop working.
I need to know whether **paid site tasks** remain after planning moves to AI.
do: Ask for **door fitting** practice while the foreman can show me the steps.
In 2032, wait on a course until **local builders confirm hiring**.
feel: **Five years** lets me prepare without rushing into a course I cannot afford.
I do not know what **retirement income** I would have after the robot date.
S3.quote: I would be around 63 when the thinking change arrives, but age alone will not tell me when I can stop working.
fieldNote: She treats the **five-year warning** as time to practise, not career security.
Retirement income is **unspecified**, so she asks about paid work rather than assuming she can stop.

steps.text: Practise door fitting or trim with supervision before 2031
Wait on a course until builders confirm hiring needs in 2032

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a decade lets people ask questions and see what work changes first. I would still not tell anyone that the later robot date makes a trade safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be around 68 when the thinking change arrives and around 71 by the robot date. I do not know what income I would have by then, and my grown-up children may have their own needs as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep learning a practical task when there is paid work and someone has time to teach me. In 2037, I would talk with my partner and grown-up children about what help we could offer each other as everyone’s plans change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years gives me a chance to watch, but it does not settle whether I can afford to stop working. The mortgage and household bills still matter now, even if the children are grown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you plan to retire by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I cannot name a retirement date without knowing what income I would have. I would talk with my partner about the numbers first, and keep working if the bills still require it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the longer warning change for your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives us time to talk before the older children are making more of their own choices. I would not assume they can support us, but we could be clear about what each of us can manage.

say: I would say **a long warning** gives families room to talk and prepare.
I would not call a trade **safe forever** because robots still arrive.
think: I will be **around 68 in 2036** and around 71 when robots arrive.
I do not know my future **retirement income**, and my grown children have needs of their own.
do: Keep learning **practical tasks** when paid work and teaching are available.
Talk in 2037 with my partner and grown children about **mutual support** as plans change.
feel: **Ten years** gives me a chance to watch, but it does not settle whether I can stop working.
I still worry about **the mortgage and bills** now.
S4.quote: I cannot name a retirement date without knowing what income I would have.
fieldNote: She values time to plan but does not assume a **pension** or fixed retirement date.
Her grown children have **their own needs**, so she does not count on their income.
Her **adult children** have their own homes, so she does not count on their income.

steps.text: Learn practical tasks through paid supervised work when available
Discuss mutual support with partner and grown children in 2037

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it gives me little time to improve before thinking work changes. Paid practice on site, clear notice about shifts and a real picture of retirement income would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I still need a fair chance to finish my working years without guessing what pays the mortgage. My partner and I have to plan with the income we actually know, not assume our grown children can carry us.

whatWouldHelp: **Paid practice** and steady shifts would help more than a course.
portrait: Kira is **58**, working as a junior construction hand while retirement is in sight.
She has **thin savings** and a mortgage, with grown-up children who have their own households.
She prefers **in-person teaching** and avoids unfamiliar technology.
She does not assume a **pension or family support** will replace wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time to improve before thinking work changes.
headlineQuote: I still need a fair chance to finish my working years without guessing what pays the mortgage.
